Thank you for the opportunity to speak
today regarding recreational backyard
fires and the potential implementation
of a regulated
pilot program similar to option C
outlined in staff report COM 2021-015.
I want to begin by acknowledging the
concerns raised in the original staff
analysis.
Safety, enforcement capacity,
environmental impact, and cost recovery
are legitimate issues. My goal is not to
dismiss those concerns, but to
demonstrate that a structured pilot
program can address them while remaining
fiscally responsible and operationally
realistic.
The core question before council is not
simply whether backyard fires should be
allowed. The real question is whether
there is a practical, enforceable
framework that balances resident demand
with safety and municipal
sustainability. I believe there is.
First, I want to address public
interest.
The engaged Waterloo survey received
over 2,400 respondents with
approximately 80% of respondents
supporting backyard recreational fires
with restrictions.
That level of support indicates this is
not a fringe issue. Residents are asking
for regulated access, not unrestricted
burnings.
Ignoring that demand does not eliminate
the issue. It simply maintains a system
where residents either go without or
travel to neighboring municipalities
where regulated programs already exist.
Second, I want to address safety.
The concerns outlined by staff regarding
smoke, nuisance complaints, and fire
spread are valid. However, those risks
are not unique to Waterloo. Multiple
municipalities manage those risks
through measurable criteria such as
setback requirements, approved burn
materials, seasonal restrictions, and
permit systems. The key here is
regulation, not prohibition.
A permit-based system ensures
accountability. Registration
requirements provide transparency for
enforcement.
Defined setbacks address property size
concerns, and seasonal or weather-based
fire bans ensure that safety remains the
priority.
Importantly, eligibility should be
determined by safety standards rather
than dwelling type. Detached,
semi-detached, or other residential
properties should qualify if they meet
measurable safety requirements. This
ensures fairness while maintaining clear
risk thresholds.
Third, I want to address enforcement.
One of the strongest arguments against
option C previously was the projected
staffing burden.
The assumption was that a new program
would require multiple dedicated staff
and significant infrastructure. However,
that assumption reflects a full-scale
operational model rather than a pilot
approach. A revised framework can
operate using complaint-based
enforcement integrated into existing
municipal enforcement and fire
prevention resources.
Digital permit applications and
automated registration systems reduce
administrative workload significantly.
Many municipalities already use online
systems for parking permits, licensing,
and registration.
The infrastructure already exists. We
don't need to breed build the program
from scratch.
Which brings me to the most crucial
point, which is cost.
The original estimate for option C
projected approximately $430,000
annually. That number, understandably,
creates concern, particularly if the
program is perceived as offering limited
municipal benefit. But a scaled model
significantly changes the financial
picture.
By reducing dedicated staffing
requirements, integrating enforcement
into existing roles, and relying on
digital administration rather than
manual processing, estimated operating
operating costs could reasonably fall
into the range of 120 to 180,000 dollars
annually. Now, when we pair that reduced
cost structure with a permit model, the
program becomes financially viable.
For example, if approximately 10,000
eligible properties participate at a
modest annual permit fee of $20, the
city could generate approximately
$200,000 annually.
Even at conservative participation
rates, this creates potential for cost
neutrality or potential cost recovery.
If the city were seeking to offset an
estimated $800,000 in pilot development
costs, permit revenue at that level
could achieve recovery in roughly 4
years.
This is important because it reframes
the program from being a financial
burden into a controlled pilot capable
of funding itself over time.
Next, I want to address operational
benefits for the city itself. Allowing
controlled burning of small quantities
of yard waste may contribute to reduced
yard waste collection volumes.
The Region of Waterloo currently charges
disposal fees per metric ton.
While backyard fires would not eliminate
yard waste services, even modest
reductions in volumes could reduce
operational pressures and associated
costs over time.
Additionally, clear regulations may
reduce ambiguous enforcement situations.
Currently, enforcement focuses on
prohibition. A regulated system creates
defined standards for compliance, making
enforcement more straightforward.
Another concern raised in the original
report was that not all properties would
qualify due to the setback requirements.
That is true, but an equity already
exists in many municipal programs. Not
every resident qualifies for every
activity. The goal is not universal
eligibility, but safe eligibility. This
ensures that only appropriate program
properties participate.
What council is ultimately being asked
to consider is not permanent policy
change today. It is a pilot program to
design to collect real data.
A pilot allows the city to measure
actual complaint volume, actual
enforcement workload, actual permit
participation, actual safety outcomes,
and actual financial performance. Right
now, many of the concerns are based on
projections rather than measured
outcomes specific to Waterloo.
A time-limited pilot reduces risk
because council remains full control
over continuation, modification, or
termination based on real evidence.
Before I conclude, I want to briefly
address timing and context. The original
2021 report indicated this issue would
be revisited. Yet, meaningful
reassessment has not yet occurred in the
years since. It is also important to
remember that the discussion of the time
took place during COVID, where there
were legitimate concerns about increased
home activity, and widespread use
creating unexpected enforcement
pressures. We are no longer in that
environment. Work patterns, social
activities, and daily routines have
largely returned to normal, which
reduces the likelihood of sudden or
excessive uptake.
Reevaluating option C allows council to
make a decision based on stable
conditions rather than pandemic era
uncertainties.
In closing, I want to bring this back to
